overview: The early Chalukyas ruled a major Deccan kingdom from Vatapi, today’s Badami. Their history includes expansion, invasion, recovery and remarkable building projects. This map’s 600 to 800 window begins after their rise and extends beyond their loss of imperial power. The later Chalukya kingdom centered on Kalyani is a different phase.

periods.title: A fortified royal center
periods.summary: Pulakeshin I established his capital at Badami; a cliff inscription of 543 records its fortification.

periods.title: Pulakeshin II’s expansion
periods.summary: The kingdom became a leading Deccan power, confronting Harsha and the Pallavas.

periods.title: Occupation and recovery
periods.summary: Pallava forces occupied Badami in 642; Chalukya rule recovered by the mid-650s.

periods.title: Renewed power and its loss
periods.summary: Royal building flourished before Rashtrakuta ascendancy ended the Badami line’s imperial rule in the 750s.

items.text: Badami’s capital occupied a dramatic setting between sandstone hills, beside a large reservoir. Pulakeshin I fortified the place in the sixth century. The landscape offered cliffs as well as built defenses, although much surviving masonry belongs to later rebuildings. A present-day fort wall cannot all be dated from one founding inscription.

Pulakeshin II expanded Chalukya authority across much of the Deccan and resisted Harsha’s advance from northern India. His success did not make the kingdom invulnerable: the Pallavas later captured Badami. The dynasty’s story includes recovery after this seventh-century disaster as well as its better-advertised victories.

Queen Lokamahadevi commissioned Pattadakal’s Virupaksha temple around 740 to commemorate her husband’s victories in the south. Monumental patronage gave a queen a lasting public presence. Her name and purpose survive alongside the king’s military reputation.

An inscription at Badami’s Jambulinga temple records Queen Vinayavati installing images of Brahma, Vishnu and Maheshvara in 699, during the reign of her son Vijayaditya. This is a specific mother-and-son royal setting in which the queen undertook her own religious foundation.

sections.title: Water, work and places to gather

items.text: Badami’s Agastya Thirtha reservoir depended on a larger water-catching landscape. A modern study identifies cliff-cut and open masonry channels from the Chalukyan period that helped direct runoff. Supplying a settlement required attention to the hills above it, not just the impressive pool at its center.

Researchers combined satellite imagery with digital models of the terrain to trace this water network. Their study separates Chalukyan channels from a much later Vijayanagara aqueduct. Small walls and channels, easily overlooked beside decorated temples, reveal how generations kept water moving where it was needed.

At Shankaralingana Gundu quarry near Pattadakal, an unfinished stone shows stages of preparation: mark a line, locate the holes, outline them, then cut them. A steel wedge and hammer found at a nearby quarry support the explanation that workers split blocks by pounding wedges into the prepared holes.

Early Chalukya stonecutters often left lens-shaped holes and U-shaped marks when blocks split. Kuppa and Menon compare these with more angular marks from later Vijayanagara work. Their proposed method helps untangle Badami’s rebuilt walls. Even the builders’ leftover dents can become historical evidence.

At Jambulinga, the porch’s outer pillars are linked by a stone bench. This small architectural feature makes a temple more than a sculpture to view from a distance: its builders provided a place to sit within the entrance space. The bench survives alongside the royal dedication.

An eighth-century Pattadakal pillar records a land transaction behind temple worship. Jnanasivacharya bought thirty nivarttanas from Aryabhatta and endowed the Vijayesvara temple. Such a record names people, a measured resource and its purpose. There is no reason to identify this landowner with the famous earlier mathematician of the same name.

Badami Cave III was dedicated in 578, before the map’s first year, by Mangalesha during Kirtivarman I’s reign. Its inscription also records the gift of a village. Carving the shrine was only one part of the project: an endowment helped connect a religious institution to resources outside its walls.

A surviving painted fragment in Cave III depicts a royal couple watching a dance. Craftsmen also left names on the cave’s facade, including Kolimanchi and Singimanchi. These details bring performers and makers into view beside the patrons; the painted court scene is not a description of every family’s entertainment.

Virupaksha’s great building project names two master architects, Gunda-Anivaritachari and Sarvasiddhi-Achari, who received royal honors. Its walls and pillars preserve stories from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Panchatantra. Skilled workers turned stone surfaces into places where familiar narratives could be recognized and retold.

Ravikirti composed the Aihole inscription of 634 or 635 and founded the Jain temple it commemorates. His Sanskrit poem praises Pulakeshin II and compares his own literary reputation with Kalidasa and Bharavi. The learned references reveal literary training; the royal praise also reminds readers that this author wanted to impress his patron.

The inscription opens jayati bhagavāñ jinendro, “Victorious is the holy Jinendra.” This is Sanskrit in scholarly Roman transliteration; the stone uses an early southern script ancestral to Kannada-Telugu writing. The short invocation comes from Ravikirti’s actual inscription, not an invented sentence for the court.

Pattadakal’s temples brought northern and southern architectural forms into the same landscape during the seventh and eighth centuries. Comparing their towers and ground plans reveals builders trying different solutions. Their contribution was a body of experiments that later architects could study and adapt.

The present monument group also contains the Jaina Narayana temple, probably built in the ninth century under the Rashtrakutas above an earlier brick Jain shrine. Its later date matters: religious construction continued after Badami Chalukya rule, and today’s cluster preserves several historical layers.

ending.text: The Rashtrakutas displaced the Badami Chalukyas as the leading Deccan power in the 750s. Political histories commonly mark 753, while ASI describes Badami’s royal phase continuing to 757. The imported 800 cutoff is later still. This transition ended a dynasty’s imperial supremacy; it did not erase the region’s communities or building traditions.
